title: Walking past a stranger
note:
Cover for an activity not built yet; the worklist alt text is the brief. Uses the outdoor block for the pavement and the foliage band.

Two things have to be true at once and they pull against each other: Lucy is WALKING, and the leash is SLACK. A walking dog is easy to draw taut, and rounds 1-19 of the tan era record exactly that failure — the leash pulled straight, which reads as pulling. So the deep J of slack is named explicitly, as is her shoulder being level with the handler's knee, which is what stopped her reading as out in front.

The stranger must be a stranger: passing behind, not interacting, not looking, not stopping. He is deliberately NOT the guest — no blue hoodie, no black cap — because the guest is a specific character who visits the house, and reusing him here would make this look like a greeting.
scene: Outdoors on a plain grey pavement with flat lawn beside it and the flat spruce foliage band behind — no building, no porch, no door, no fence and no road anywhere in the picture. The handler WALKS from left to right in profile, upright and easy. Lucy walks at her side on the near hand, in profile, moving with her: her SHOULDER IS LEVEL WITH THE HANDLER'S KNEE and her nose is not further forward than the handler's leading foot — she is beside her, never ahead of her. Lucy's head is up and her whole muzzle is tipped up toward the handler's face; her ears are up, her tail level, her gait relaxed. THE LEASH IS ATTACHED AND SLACK: its clip is closed on the D-ring at the front of her collar, and the line runs from that ring up to the handler's near hand held low, hanging in a deep obvious J of slack along the way — it is never straight and never taut, because a taut line reads as pulling. Follow it with your eye from collar to hand without a break. BEHIND THEM, a stranger walks the other way in the background, small and well back — an ordinary adult in muted neutral clothes, NOT in a blue hoodie and NOT in a black cap, because that is the household's guest and this is not him. He is not looking at Lucy, not stopping, not reaching, not interacting: he is simply passing. Neither Lucy nor the handler is looking at him. HOW BIG THEY ARE DRAWN: draw the figures SMALLER than the composition wants, grouped close together near the middle rather than spread across the frame. The top of the highest head sits about a QUARTER of the way down from the top edge and no higher; the lowest thing that matters no lower than three quarters of the way down. Above every head leave a clear band of empty background at least a fifth of the picture height with nothing in it, and below them clear empty ground. Left and right, nothing that matters enters the outer eighth of the width. The app crops this two ways at once — a wide Today band keeping only the middle strip of the HEIGHT, and a centred square keeping only the middle three-quarters of the WIDTH — so a head near the top edge is decapitated on the app largest surface. Empty background above them is better than a sliced head.
mustBeTrue: the leash is visibly clipped to the D-ring at the front of Lucy's collar and hangs in a deep J of slack all the way to the handler's low hand, never straight or taut; Lucy's shoulder is level with the handler's knee with her nose no further forward than the handler's leading foot, and her muzzle is tipped up toward the handler's face; the stranger is small, well behind them, in muted neutral clothes rather than a blue hoodie or black cap, and is passing without looking at or interacting with either of them; and the top of the handler's head sits about a quarter of the way down the frame with clear background above it and nothing that matters in the top fifth, the bottom quarter or the outer eighth of either side.
